note.text:
On the graph of y = ax² + bx + c, the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 are the x-coordinates where the curve crosses the x-axis (y = 0).
To solve ax² + bx + c = k with the same graph, draw the horizontal line y = k and read the x-coordinates where it meets the curve.
To solve a different quadratic, rearrange it as (the graphed expression) = (a straight line), draw that line, and read the crossings.
Example: with y = x² − 2x − 3 drawn, x² − 3x − 1 = 0 becomes x² − 2x − 3 = x − 2: draw y = x − 2.
Graph readings are approximate; give them to the nearest grid line or as the question asks.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to read the roots of a quadratic equation from its graph and solve related equations by drawing a straight line.
Builds on: Lesson {23} (drawing parabolas) and Lesson {20} (crossings of graphs).
Leads to: intersections of curves and lines in Form Five, and solving equations that algebra cannot.

sections.heading: Roots on the x-axis
sections.text:
The graph of y = {quad(1, -2, -3)} crosses the x-axis at x = {-1} and x = {3}.
On the x-axis y = {0}, so these x values make {quad(1, -2, -3)} = {0}: they are the roots.
Check: ({-1})² − {2} × ({-1}) − {3} = {1} + {2} − {3} = {0}.
If the curve crosses between grid lines, estimate: x ≈ {2.6}, for example.

sections.heading: Other equations with the same graph
sections.text:
To solve {quad(1, -2, -3)} = {5}, draw the horizontal line y = {5}. It meets the curve at x = {-2} and x = {4}.
To solve x² − {mono(3, 'x')} − {1} = {0}, make the left side match the graph:
x² − {mono(3, 'x')} − {1} = {0} is the same as {quad(1, -2, -3)} = x − {2} (add x − {2} to both sides).
So draw y = x − {2} and read the x values where it crosses the curve.

key_words.meaning: an answer read from a graph
read as closely as the grid allows

mistake.wrong: to solve {quad(1, -2, -3)} = {5}, read where the curve crosses the x-axis
mistake.right: draw y = {5} and read where it meets the curve
mistake.why: The x-axis is y = {0}. For = {5}, use the line y = {5}.

worked_example.problem: The graph of y = {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)} is drawn. Use it to solve {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)} = {k}.
steps: Read the x-coordinates where it meets the curve: x = {-2} and x = {4}.

cards.idea: The roots of ax² + bx + c = {0} are where the graph crosses the x-axis.
example: y = {quad(1, -2, -3)} crosses at x = {-1} and x = {3}

cards.idea: To solve ax² + bx + c = k, draw the line y = k and read where it meets the curve.
example: {quad(1, -2, -3)} = {5}: y = {5} meets the curve at x = {-2} and x = {4}

check.prompt: The graph of y = {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)} is drawn. Which line do you draw to solve {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)} = {k}?

misconceptions.explain: The equation says the expression equals {k}: draw y = {k}.
x = {k} is a vertical line: it gives only one point on the curve, not the solutions.
The right side is just the number {k}, so the line is horizontal.

solution: The left side is the graphed expression y. So y = {k}.
Draw the horizontal line y = {k} and read where it meets the curve.
So the answer is {answer}.

cards.idea: For another equation, rearrange it as (the graphed expression) = (a line), and draw the line.

check.prompt: The graph of y = {quad(1, b, c)} is drawn. Which straight line must you draw to solve {quad(1, b2, c2)} = {0}?

misconceptions.explain: Move the terms the right way: x² + {mono(b, 'x')} + {c} − ({poly([b - b2, 'x'], [c - c2, ''])}) must give {quad(1, b2, c2)}.
Subtract the two quadratics: the line is the difference, not the new x and number terms.
y = {0} solves {quad(1, b, c)} = {0}, a different equation.

solution: Rearrange so that the left side is the graphed expression: {quad(1, b2, c2)} = {0}.
Add {poly([b - b2, 'x'], [c - c2, ''])} to both sides: {quad(1, b, c)} = {poly([b - b2, 'x'], [c - c2, ''])}.
So draw y = {poly([b - b2, 'x'], [c - c2, ''])}.

questions.prompt: The graph shows y = {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)}. What are the roots of {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)} = {0}?

misconceptions.explain: Read the crossings off the x-axis: they are at {p} and {q}.
{p * q} is where the curve meets the y-axis, not the x-axis.
That is the axis of symmetry, halfway between the roots.

solution: The roots are where the curve crosses the x-axis.
It crosses at x = {p} and x = {q}.
So the answer is {answer}.

questions.prompt: The graph shows y = {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)}. Use it to find the larger root of {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)} = {0}.

misconceptions.explain: {p * q} is the y-intercept. The roots are on the x-axis.

solution: Look for where the curve crosses the x-axis.
The crossings are at x = {p} and x = {q}.
The larger root is {answer}.

questions.prompt: The graph of y = {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)} is drawn. Which line do you draw to solve {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)} = {k}?

misconceptions.explain: The equation says the expression equals {k}: draw y = {k}.
x = {k} is a vertical line: it gives only one point on the curve, not the solutions.
The right side is just the number {k}, so the line is horizontal.

solution: The left side is the graphed expression y. So y = {k}.
Draw the horizontal line y = {k} and read where it meets the curve.
So the answer is {answer}.

questions.prompt: The graph of y = {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)} is drawn. Draw y = {t * t - (p + q) * t + p * q} and use it to solve {quad(1, -(p + q), p * q)} = {t * t - (p + q) * t + p * q}. Give the larger solution.

misconceptions.explain: {q} is a root of the curve = {0}. Here the curve equals {t * t - (p + q) * t + p * q}.

solution: The line y = {t * t - (p + q) * t + p * q} meets the curve at x = {t} and x = {p + q - t} (symmetric about x = {(p + q) / 2}).
Check x = {t}: {t * t} − {(p + q) * t} + {br(p * q)} = {t * t - (p + q) * t + p * q}.
The larger solution is {answer}.
where: abs(t * t - (p + q) * t + p * q) <= 8
